lessons.title: Design and Construction of Ox-Drawn Ploughs
lessons.body: An ox-drawn plough is the backbone of animal-powered farming. You will need mild steel for the frame, a hardened steel share, and a mouldboard. Start with the beam: a straight piece of hardwood or steel pipe, 1.8â2.2 m long, 8â10 cm diameter. The beam connects the yoke to the plough body. Next, the handles: two wooden or steel shafts, 1.2 m long, set at a comfortable angle for the operator to walk behind. The body includes the frog (where share and mouldboard meet), the share (the cutting point), and the mouldboard (which turns the soil). For a 20 cm plough, use a share 25 cm long, 5 cm wide at the point, tapering to 10 cm at the base. Hardened steel from old truck leaf springs works well. Heat the share to cherry red (850â900Â°C) and quench in oil to harden. The mouldboard can be made from 3 mm mild steel sheet, curved to a radius of about 30 cm. Bolt all parts with 12 mm bolts for easy replacement. The hitch point should be adjustable to set depth: move it up for shallow ploughing, down for deeper. Test in loose soil first. Adjust the landside (a flat piece on the side) to keep the plough straight. A well-built plough should turn a furrow 15â20 cm deep and 25â30 cm wide with a single ox or a pair of donkeys. Remember to grease the hitch pin regularly.

lessons.title: Making Harrows and Cultivators
lessons.body: Harrows and cultivators prepare seedbeds and control weeds. A spike harrow is simplest: a rectangular frame of 5 cm angle iron, 1.5 m wide and 1 m long. Weld or bolt 12â16 steel spikes (1 cm diameter, 15 cm long) in staggered rows. The spikes should angle back slightly to avoid clogging. For a disc harrow, use old car wheel hubs and discs (e.g., from a disc plough) mounted on a shaft. Space discs 20 cm apart, angled 15â20 degrees to cut and turn soil. A cultivator (or tined cultivator) has curved tines made from 1.5 cm spring steel. Bend tines to a sweep shape: 30 cm long, curving forward. Mount 5â7 tines on a toolbar with clamps. For row crop cultivation, adjust tine spacing to match your crop rows (e.g., 75 cm for maize). Use a depth wheel to control how deep tines goâset it to 10â15 cm for weeding. Build a hitch that allows the implement to follow the oxen without swinging. All joints should be welded or bolted with 10 mm bolts. Paint with red oxide primer then enamel to prevent rust. Test on dry soil first: if tines bounce, add weight (a stone or metal block) on the frame. A good harrow leaves a level, fine seedbed; a cultivator uproots weeds without burying small crops.

lessons.title: Crafting Yokes and Harnesses
lessons.body: A yoke transfers the animal's pulling power to the implement. For oxen, use a neck yoke: a straight wooden bar 1.2â1.5 m long, 10â12 cm diameter, made from tough wood like mukwa or mvule. Shape it with an axe and smooth with a spokeshave. The yoke sits across the necks of a pair of oxen. Carve two U-shaped bows (also wood) that go under the neck and attach to the yoke with wooden pegs or metal pins. The bows should be loose enough to allow the animal to breathe but tight enough not to slip. For donkeys, use a breast collar harness: a padded leather or canvas strap that goes across the chest, attached to traces (ropes or chains) that pull the implement. Make the collar from 5 cm wide leather, stuffed with straw or foam for comfort. The traces should be 3â4 m long, made from 8 mm wire rope or heavy chain. For a single animal, use a swingletree (a wooden bar) to balance the pull. All harness parts must be smooth to prevent chafing. Check daily for wear. For yokes, drill holes for pegs with a 12 mm bit. Treat wood with used engine oil to repel termites. A well-fitted yoke lets an ox pull 500â800 kg; a poor one causes sores and reduces power by half.

lessons.title: Making Cart and Wagon Parts
lessons.body: Carts and wagons need strong wheels, axles, and a sturdy body. For a two-wheel cart, start with the axle: a 5 cm solid steel rod, 1.5 m long. Weld a hub (10 cm diameter pipe, 15 cm long) at each end. The wheels can be wooden spoked or steel disc. For wooden wheels, use 8 spokes of 4 cm hardwood, a felloe (rim) of 1.2 m diameter, and an iron tyre shrunk on. Heat the iron tyre to 300Â°C and drop it over the rim; it shrinks tight as it cools. For steel wheels, cut two discs from 6 mm plate, 1 m diameter, and weld a 10 cm pipe hub in the centre. The cart body: a platform 2 m long, 1.2 m wide, made from 5 cm planks or steel sheet. Add sides 30 cm high for carrying loads. The shafts (for hitching to animals) should be 2.5 m long, 8 cm diameter, attached to the axle with U-bolts. Use a turntable for a four-wheel wagon: a circle of steel with a kingpin, allowing the front axle to pivot. Load capacity: a two-wheel cart with 1 m wheels can carry 500â800 kg on flat ground. Grease wheel bearings every 50 km. Check all bolts weekly. Replace worn bushes in the hubs with bronze or nylon.

lessons.title: Repairing Animal-Drawn Equipment
lessons.body: Breakdowns happen. Learn to fix common problems fast. For ploughs: a dull share is the most common issue. Remove it, heat to 850Â°C, and re-shape with a hammer on an anvil. Quench in oil. If the share is cracked, weld it with a 3.2 mm electrode, then grind smooth. For harrows: bent tines can be straightened cold with a heavy hammer, but if cracked, replace. Keep spare tines. For yokes: cracked wood can be repaired with a steel plate and bolts, but if the crack is deep, replace the yoke. For carts: loose wheel bearings cause wobble. Remove the wheel, knock out the old bearing, and press in a new one (use a socket and hammer). If the axle is bent, heat it red and straighten on a flat surface. For harnesses: replace worn leather straps with new ones; stitch with waxed thread and a saddler's needle. Always carry a repair kit: spare bolts (8, 10, 12 mm), wire, pliers, a file, and a hacksaw. Before each use, inspect for cracks, loose bolts, and worn parts. Fix small problems before they become big. A 30-minute repair in the evening saves a day of lost work. Teach yourself to weld if you canâmany villages have a welder who can help.

lessons.title: Safety and Ergonomics in Animal-Drawn Tools
lessons.body: Animal-drawn tools can injure you or your animals if used carelessly. Always wear sturdy boots, long trousers, and gloves when handling implements. When hitching, stand to the side, never between the animal and the implement. Use a halter and lead rope to control the animal; never wrap ropes around your handâif the animal bolts, you could lose a finger. Keep blades sharp: a dull share requires more force, tiring both you and the animal. For ergonomics, adjust handles to your height: when standing, your elbows should be slightly bent. The plough handles should be at hip level. If you must bend, you will get back pain. For the animal, ensure the yoke or collar fits wellâcheck for sores daily. Pad collars with cloth if needed. Work at a steady pace; oxen walk at 1â1.5 m/s. Take breaks every hour. When lifting heavy parts (wheels, plough bodies), bend your knees, not your back. Use a cart or wheelbarrow to move heavy items. Keep your work area clear of tools and rocks. Store implements under cover to prevent rust and damage. Teach children to stay away from animals and moving equipment. A safe farmer is a productive farmer.

lessons.title: Practical Reference
lessons.body:
Practical Reference: Animal-Drawn Implement Making

This Practical Reference is the working bench companion for the module Animal-Drawn Implement Making. It is written for artisans, small-scale manufacturers, and agripreneurs who build, sell, repair, and hire out ox-drawn equipment across Africa. The focus is business-first: every measurement, joint, and material choice below is framed around what makes a tool stronger, cheaper to produce, easier to repair, and more sellable to farmers. Whether you are welding ploughs in a roadside workshop in Mbeya or assembling harrows for a cooperative in Kaduna, the principles are the sameâbuild for the soil, the animal, and the customer's wallet.

Animal traction remains the backbone of smallholder cultivation across sub-Saharan Africa. According to FAO, animal-drawn implements are used on a significant share of cultivated land in countries such as Ethiopia, Tanzania, Kenya, Mali, and Zimbabwe, and demand for locally manufactured tools continues to grow as farmers seek affordable alternatives to tractors. For the artisan, this is a market opportunity: a well-made ox plough that can be repaired locally will outsell an imported unit that cannot.

Core Design Principles for All Implements

Before looking at individual tools, internalise these five principles. They apply to ploughs, harrows, cultivators, yokes, and carts alike.

1. Match the tool to the soil and the animal. A light sandy soil needs a different plough body than heavy clay. A pair of oxen weighing 500â700 kg can pull a plough with a 20â25 cm furrow width; donkeys need lighter, narrower implements. Overloading animals reduces work output and shortens their working lifeâa direct cost to your customer.

2. Build for local repair. Use standard bolts, flat bar, and angle iron that a village welder can replace. Avoid proprietary castings that must be imported. A tool that can be fixed in a day is worth more than one that sits idle for a month.

3. Standardise your parts. If you produce ten ploughs a month, use the same beam length, the same share pattern, and the same yoke dimensions. Standardisation cuts production time, reduces waste, and lets you sell spare partsâa high-margin side business.

4. Control weight. Every kilogram of implement weight is a kilogram the animal must pull. Use the lightest section that gives the required strength. A typical ox plough beam is 1.2â1.5 m long and made from 50 Ã 50 mm hardwood or 40 Ã 40 mm steel box section.

5. Design for the operator. Handles must be at a comfortable height (about 90â110 cm for an adult), with grips that do not blister hands. Ergonomics is not a luxuryâit determines whether a farmer can work a full day and whether they recommend your tool to neighbours.

Design and Construction of Ox-Drawn Ploughs

The ox plough is the highest-volume animal-drawn implement in most African markets. The standard mouldboard plough consists of a beam, a body (mouldboard and share), two handles, and a hitch point. Key dimensions for a medium ox plough:

  • Beam length: 1.2â1.5 m, hardwood (e.g., Pterocarpus or Brachystegia) or steel box section
  • Share width: 20â25 cm for oxen; 12â18 cm for donkeys
  • Mouldboard: curved steel plate, 3â5 mm thick, radius matched to soil type
  • Handles: 90â110 cm above ground, spaced 40â50 cm apart
  • Hitch: adjustable vertical and horizontal clevis for depth and line of pull control

The share is the wear partâmake it replaceable. A bolt-on share that a farmer can swap in the field is a strong selling point. Harden the cutting edge by quenching in used engine oil, or source recycled spring steel from vehicle leaf springs, which is widely available and holds an edge well.

Making Harrows and Cultivators

Harrows break clods and level seedbeds; cultivators weed between rows. Both are lighter than ploughs and use tines or discs mounted on a frame. A typical ox-drawn spike-tooth harrow uses a 1.5â2.0 m hardwood or steel frame with 9â15 tines set at 15â20 cm spacing. Cultivators use 3â5 sweeps or tines mounted on a toolbar, with adjustable spacing to match row width (commonly 60â90 cm for maize).

Business tip: harrows and cultivators share the same frame and hitch system as your plough. If you standardise the hitch, a farmer can buy one yoke and hitch assembly and use it across three implements. That increases your average sale value per customer.

Crafting Yokes and Harnesses

The yoke transfers the animal's power to the implement. A poorly fitted yoke causes sores, reduces pulling efficiency, and loses you customers. The head yoke (neck yoke) is common for oxen in southern and eastern Africa; the withers yoke is used in West Africa. Key specification: the yoke must sit comfortably on the neck or withers without pinching, and the eye spacing must match the animal pair.

Use seasoned hardwood (e.g., Acacia, Combretum) or welded steel. Pad contact points with leather or canvas. Harness chains and traces should be rated well above the expected pullâa pair of oxen can exert 1.5â2.5 kN of draught force, so use chain with a safe working load of at least 5 kN.

Making Cart and Wagon Parts

Ox carts are a high-value product for transport of harvest, water, and inputs. Key parts to manufacture locally:

  • Axle and bearings: use sealed roller bearings where affordable; otherwise hardwood bushes with grease nipples. A 1.5â2 tonne cart needs an axle of at least 40 mm solid steel.
  • Wheels: steel rims with pneumatic tyres reduce draught on rough ground. Wooden spoked wheels are cheaper but need regular maintenance.
  • Shafts and singletree: shafts 2.0â2.4 m long, angled so the cart balances with the load centred over the axle.
  • Body: hardwood planks or welded steel frame with a wooden deck. Keep the centre of gravity low to prevent overturning.

Carts are a strong business line because they can be sold or rented. A well-built cart that can carry 1.5 tonnes and be repaired locally will generate hire income for years.

Repairing Animal-Drawn Equipment

Repair is recurring revenue. Build a repair kit and a simple diagnostic routine:

  1. Inspect the share and mouldboard for wear; replace or re-edge.
  2. Check beam for cracks, especially at the body joint; reinforce with steel plate if needed.
  3. Check yoke and harness for cracks, worn padding, and stretched chain.
  4. Check all bolts and pins; replace with galvanised or stainless where possible.
  5. Check wheel bearings and axle play on carts; repack or replace bearings.
  6. Test the tool in the field before returning it to the customer.

Offer a service contract: annual inspection and share replacement for a fixed fee. This builds loyalty and smooths your cash flow.

Safety and Ergonomics in Animal-Drawn Tools

Animal traction injuries are common and preventable. The main risks are cuts from shares and discs, crushing from overturning carts, and back and shoulder strain from poor handle design. Train your customers on safe use, and build safety into the tool.

â  SAFETY WARNING â Sharp Edges and Animal Handling

Shares, discs, and cultivator tines are sharp and can cause severe lacerations. Always fit transport guards or wrap blades during storage and transport. Never allow children to handle or hitch animals unattended. When hitching, keep hands clear of the yoke eye and traces; use a quick-release hitch so the animal can be freed if it panics. Wear closed shoes and eye protection when sharpening or welding. Ensure animals are properly trained and handled by an adult at all times. A panicked ox can overturn a cart and cause fatal crushing injuries.

Ergonomic improvements that cost little but add value: rubber or leather handle grips, adjustable handle height, balanced tool weight, and a hitch that lets the operator walk to the side rather than directly behind the animal. These reduce fatigue and injury, and they are selling points you can demonstrate to buyers.

Data Tables

Sources: FAO, Farm Implements for Animal Traction; FAO/CTA, Animal Traction in Africa; and field data from regional animal traction programmes (e.g., ATNESA/FAO training materials). Figures are indicative and vary with soil, animal condition, and operator skill.

Sources: FAO, Farm Implements for Animal Traction; ILO/FAO, Ergonomic Guidelines for Animal Traction; and manufacturer practice from small-scale implement workshops in East and West Africa.

Quick Reference Checklist

  • â Confirm the target animal (ox, donkey, cow) and soil type before designing.
  • â Use standard, locally available materials and bolt sizes for easy repair.
  • â Make the share replaceable and harden the cutting edge.
  • â Standardise beam, hitch, and yoke dimensions across your product range.
  • â Fit padded, well-fitted yokes and quick-release hitches.
  • â Add handle grips and check handle height for operator comfort.
  • â Field-test every implement before delivery and train the buyer on safe use.
  • â Offer a repair and spare-parts service to build recurring revenue.

Further Reading (Free Official Resources)

  • FAO â Farm Implements for Animal Traction (FAO Land and Water Division; full text online).
  • FAO â Draught Animal Power Manual (FAO, Rome; covers implements, yokes, and harnesses).
  • FAO/CTA â Animal Traction in Africa (training and technical guidance).
  • ILO â Ergonomic Guidelines for Animal Traction (PDF; safety and ergonomics).
  • ATNESA â Animal Traction Network for Eastern and Southern Africa (conference papers and technical notes).

quiz.q: What is the ideal length for an ox-drawn plough beam?
quiz.explanation: A beam of 1.8â2.2 m provides proper leverage and clearance for the animals.

quiz.q: Which material is best for making a plough share?
options: C) Hardened steel from leaf springs
quiz.explanation: Hardened steel from old truck leaf springs is tough and can be heat-treated for wear resistance.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of the mouldboard on a plough?
options: B) To turn the soil over
quiz.explanation: The mouldboard lifts and turns the furrow slice, burying weeds and aerating soil.

quiz.q: How deep should a typical ox-drawn plough turn soil?
quiz.explanation: A depth of 15â20 cm is suitable for most crops and matches the power of a pair of oxen.

quiz.q: What is the main function of a spike harrow?
quiz.explanation: Spike harrows break clods and level the seedbed after ploughing.

quiz.q: How many spikes are typical for a 1.5 m wide spike harrow?
quiz.explanation: 12â16 spikes in staggered rows provide good coverage without clogging.

quiz.q: What angle should disc harrow discs be set to?
quiz.explanation: 15â20 degrees allows the discs to cut and turn soil effectively.

quiz.q: For row crop cultivation, tine spacing should match:
quiz.explanation: Tines must be spaced to avoid damaging crop rows while uprooting weeds between them.

quiz.q: What is a common material for making cultivator tines?
quiz.explanation: Spring steel tines are flexible and strong, resisting breakage in rocky soil.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of a depth wheel on a cultivator?
quiz.explanation: A depth wheel limits how deep tines penetrate, ensuring consistent cultivation.

quiz.q: Which wood is recommended for making a yoke?
quiz.explanation: Mukwa and mvule are tough, durable hardwoods that resist cracking under load.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of the bows on a neck yoke?
options: B) To go under the animal's neck and hold the yoke
quiz.explanation: Bows secure the yoke around the neck without choking the animal.

quiz.q: For a breast collar harness, what material is best for comfort?
options: B) Leather or canvas padded with foam
quiz.explanation: Padded leather or canvas distributes pressure and prevents chafing.

quiz.q: How long should traces be for a breast collar harness?
quiz.explanation: 3â4 m traces allow the animal to pull without the implement hitting its heels.

quiz.q: What is a swingletree used for?
options: A) To balance the pull of a single animal
quiz.explanation: A swingletree equalizes the pull and reduces side forces on a single animal.

quiz.q: How can you protect a wooden yoke from termites?
options: B) Treat with used engine oil
quiz.explanation: Used engine oil repels termites and moisture, extending yoke life.

quiz.q: What is the typical load capacity of a two-wheel cart with 1 m wheels?
quiz.explanation: A well-built two-wheel cart can carry 500â800 kg on flat ground.

quiz.q: How is an iron tyre fitted to a wooden wheel?
quiz.explanation: Heating expands the tyre; it shrinks tight as it cools, holding the wheel together.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of a turntable on a four-wheel wagon?
options: B) To allow the front axle to pivot
quiz.explanation: A turntable lets the front wheels steer, making the wagon turn easily.

quiz.q: How often should wheel bearings be greased?
quiz.explanation: Greasing every 50 km prevents wear and overheating of bearings.

quiz.q: What is the most common repair needed on a plough?
quiz.explanation: The share wears quickly; sharpening or replacing it is a frequent task.

quiz.q: How can you straighten a bent harrow tine?
options: A) Heat it red and bend
quiz.explanation: Cold hammering is quick and preserves the tine's temper if done carefully.

quiz.q: What should you do if a wooden yoke has a deep crack?
quiz.explanation: A deep crack weakens the yoke and can break under load, risking injury.

quiz.q: What is a good repair kit item for animal-drawn equipment?
quiz.explanation: Spare bolts of various sizes allow quick fixes for loose parts.

quiz.q: Why should you inspect equipment before each use?
options: B) To catch small problems early
quiz.explanation: Early detection prevents breakdowns and accidents during work.

quiz.q: What should you wear when handling animal-drawn implements?
quiz.explanation: Boots and gloves protect feet and hands from cuts and crushing.

quiz.q: Where should you stand when hitching an animal to an implement?
options: D) In front of the animal
quiz.explanation: Standing to the side avoids being crushed if the animal moves suddenly.

quiz.q: How should you adjust plough handles for good ergonomics?
options: B) At hip level with slightly bent elbows
quiz.explanation: Hip-level handles with bent elbows reduce back strain and improve control.

quiz.q: What is the recommended walking speed for oxen?
quiz.explanation: Oxen work best at a steady 1â1.5 m/s, matching their natural pace.

quiz.q: How can you prevent back injury when lifting heavy parts?
quiz.explanation: Bending knees keeps the load close and uses leg muscles, protecting the back.
